articles.description: When wildfire risk is high, utilities sometimes shut off power lines, leaving people without electricity for days.
paragraphs: When it’s extremely windy and dry, and the risk of wildfire is high, utilities sometimes turn off certain power lines to prevent sparking a blaze.
Brooks: “I live in Boulder, Colorado. We had our power turned off for five days last December. … The only saving grace for us was that it was relatively temperate and so pipes weren’t freezing.”
That’s Cameron Brooks of the group Think Microgrid . He says microgrids can help prevent those outages.

A microgrid is an energy system that provides power to a building, a neighborhood, or an area like a college campus. It often includes solar panels and battery storage. And it’s connected to the larger electricity grid, but it can also disconnect and operate independently.
So microgrids can provide backup power when the grid goes down during storms or when utilities need to shut off power to specific lines.
Brooks: “Then the utility could safely deenergize those lines, avoid the risk of wildfire, without causing a disruption to service that people depend on.”
So microgrids can help build resilience in wildfire-prone areas while also expanding the use of clean, renewable energy.

paragraphs: The small fire slowly licked its way through a dense growth of pine trees in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains of northern New Mexico. A team of federal employees moved in tandem with the flames, dropping more fire from drip torches to clear out the small trees, deadwood, scrub and grasses that could fuel a runaway blaze in the future. Everything seemed to be going to plan.

But come afternoon, strong winds swept into the burn area. Powerful gusts carried the carefully planned fire beyond the control line intended to contain it. By 5 p.m. on April 6, 2022, the U.S. Forest Service reported the burn had escaped its control and declared it a wildfire.

The Hermit’s Peak Fire would eventually merge with another prescribed burn that had survived the winter as a “sleeper” fire in nearby Calf Canyon. In January, the Forest Service had burned piles of tree trunks and limbs left over from previous forest-thinning operations. But embers from the pile burn had smoldered beneath the winter snow and the fire reemerged in the spring.

By the time the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon Fire finally came under control in August 2022, the once-modest prescribed burns intended to reduce the potential for megafires in New Mexico had become the largest wildfire in the state’s history.

The colossal fire swept across more than 340,000 acres and destroyed more than 900 structures in San Miguel, Mora and Taos counties. Torrential rain in the fire’s burn scar spawned a flash flood that killed three people.

articles.title: Twenty Years of Watts Up With That?
articles.description: Twenty years ago today, I started Watts Up With That with one simple blog entry. The idea was somewhat gee-whiz in nature. It did not stay that way for long.
paragraphs: Twenty years, over 600 million page views, over 38,000 articles, countless arguments, personal losses, and one stubborn idea: scientific claims should stand or fall on the evidence.

Twenty years ago, on November 17, 2006, I published the first post at Watts Up With That? . I had no grand plan to build one of the world’s most widely read climate-related websites. I certainly didn’t envision spending the next two decades examining temperature records, questioning climate models, debating scientists, dealing with the occasional internet mob, or explaining for the umpteenth time why a thermometer next to an air-conditioning exhaust might not be the ideal instrument for measuring long-term climate change. I thought I might finally have a little spare time. That prediction turned out to be spectacularly wrong, and considering the subject matter that would eventually dominate this website, there’s a certain irony in that.

The original idea behind WUWT was simple enough. I wanted a place to discuss interesting things about science, technology, weather, and the natural world. I described it as somewhat “gee-whiz” in nature. The internet already had plenty of celebrity gossip and political shouting matches, and I was more interested in the kind of useful trivia that makes people stop and think. Why is the sky blue during the day but black at night? Why does urine smell funny after eating asparagus? And, with apologies to Lon, does disc golf cause cancer? Those were the sorts of questions I thought we might explore. The only real ground rules were to avoid crude language and personal attacks. Otherwise, almost anything was fair game.

The blog began under the umbrella of the Chico Enterprise-Record’s NorCalBlogs platform, and my intended audience was largely local: people around Northern California who knew me from my days on television and shared my interest in science, weather, and technology. For the first few months, that’s pretty much what it was. I wrote about PlayStation 3s, internet speed tests , hurricane-strength nails, and household power hogs. Climate-related material appeared almost immediately, but WUWT was still primarily a general science and technology blog. That began to change in the spring of 2007, when a longstanding curiosity about weather instruments led me in an unexpected direction.

Before getting into that history, I should say a word about the feature image created for this anniversary by Charles Rotter. Charles has taken the familiar Stevenson screen, that traditional white wooden shelter used to house weather instruments, and given it a rather unusual architectural upgrade. It now resembles an outhouse, complete with a thermometer mounted on the door, standing alone in a field beneath a beautiful sunrise. The caption simply reads, “TWENTY YEARS — 2006–2026.”

I had to laugh when I first saw it. After two decades of examining the condition and placement of surface temperature stations, the image sums up rather neatly what we’ve thought about the quality of some of the measurements being used to construct the historical temperature record. The thermometer may be housed in something that looks vaguely official, but that doesn’t necessarily make the observations trustworthy. Of course, the cartoon is deliberately exaggerated, and the actual scientific questions are considerably more complicated. Still, Charles has managed to convey twenty years of frustration with poorly sited instruments in a single picture. Sometimes a little humor gets the point across more effectively than another hundred pages of statistical analysis. Thanks, Charles. It’s a fitting image for the occasion.
articles.lede: Twenty years ago today, I started Watts Up With That with one simple blog entry. The idea was somewhat gee-whiz in nature.

articles.title: A Landmark Deal Saved Colorado’s Roan Plateau. Now It’s Headed Back to the Auction Block.
articles.description: A new federal mandate requires fossil fuel lease auctions on land that past negotiations were supposed to have set aside, raising concerns about the fate of other public lands protections.
paragraphs: Almost a decade after a compromise between the Bureau of Land Management, conservationists and local governments safeguarded about 90 percent of the Roan Plateau in Western Colorado from gas drilling, those federal protections are being unraveled in the Trump administration’s push to open more public lands for resource extraction.

But in 2012, a U.S. District Court judge in Denver ruled the agency hadn’t followed proper protocol in developing the leasing plan and ordered that it be updated after the BLM conducted additional analysis of air quality impacts and considered an alternate plan, the “Community Alternative.” After two more years of litigation, the plaintiffs and the BLM reached a settlement in 2014 that canceled all but two leases on top of the plateau.

Those protections are now in doubt. The second Trump administration’s push to increase resource extraction on public lands has reopened the possibility of development on lands that were previously protected. This December, the Bureau of Land Management will offer four parcels atop the Roan as part of the quarterly statewide lease sales mandated by 2025’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

“There was such broad consensus on the ground in this local community to protect this very special place,” said Chris Winter, a natural resources and environmental lawyer who runs the University of Colorado Law School’s Getches-Wilkinson Center for Natural Resources, Energy, and the Environment. “And then the administration can come in and just override that local consensus. I think that should concern everybody across the West.”

“There’s nobody out here who lives out here who wants to ruin the land,” said Wade Haerle, Executive Director of Club 20, a Western Slope advocacy organization that promotes resource development as essential for area economies. “We have been in support of leasing it as soon as practical … and we firmly believe that hunting and fishing, and oil and gas, [are all appropriate uses of] public lands, and they can coexist together.”

The Roan Plateau rises 3,500 feet above the Colorado River Valley between De Beque and Rifle on Colorado’s Western Slope. It sits atop the southern margin of the Piceance Basin, one of the most heavily drilled natural gas fields in the West; the federal land at the center of the fight covers some 73,600 acres.

articles.title: Can this experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?
articles.description: Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests
paragraphs: O n Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought . Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come.

Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider , which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable.
The trials aim to identify robust apple varieties that are resistant to diseases and pests, crop reliably and can withstand the most extreme weather that might affect Somerset .

“Somerset is the best county in the world for making cider. But the climate is changing. It has been changing for a long time. We need to be in a position where we’ve got the experience, the knowledge and the trees in place to deal with those changes,” says Martin Thatcher, the company’s managing director.

One of the biggest challenges he faces is the length of time it takes to introduce a new apple variety and change growing methods in orchards. “It doesn’t happen overnight. Each apple tree takes seven years to get to a fruit crop and could last 40 years. So it takes a very long time [for experiments] to come to fruition,” he says.

The trials came about because, nearly 30 years ago, his father, John Thatcher, rescued 458 varieties of cider apples grown at the Long Ashton research station, a government-funded horticultural and agricultural research centre founded in 1903. “My father took cuttings of every single variety before the centre was closed down, so we have an orchard with 458 varieties in it.”

The collection includes traditional cider apples and newer varieties that cater for modern tastes. “We’re looking at that orchard now and first of all seeing which apples make fabulous cider. And then we’re looking at how the trees are doing under modern orchard conditions – and if they’re good healthy trees and they’re cropping, we will plant them out in rows of 100-tree trials, to future-proof our orchard growing.”

He is trying to use fewer pesticides, so is keen to find varieties that are naturally resistant to disease and pests, and will blossom at exactly the moment when spring conditions suit apple tree pollinators such as bumblebees and honeybees.

Another priority is to find varieties that need less winter chill in a warming climate: apple trees, he explains, need a sustained cold period in winter to complete their dormancy, which enables their fruit buds to develop properly in spring. “That winter chill is really important – and last year, we probably didn’t have quite enough, and some varieties are more susceptible to a lack of winter chill than others.”
articles.lede: O n Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought.

articles.description: In the end, to me, the weather and climate have to be stand-alones, and the other items are a response to them, not the reason for an answer.
paragraphs: I really wanted to be involved in the hierarchy that would help figure out how to address the climate agenda. I felt that, as someone who has been forecasting for over 50 years and relies on climate and past weather data, I could offer a different kind of input — one from the guy digging the ditch who has to deal with the fact that being wrong actually costs you something. I have always felt that the crucible of capitalism and competition will yield the best results. And certainly, in a private sector that has to compete for a shrinking dollar, you cannot simply dismiss anything that may impact the forecast.

But now I am glad I am not involved. And that is a horrible thing to say, because of the reason. It has to do with what I was warning my colleagues about at the climate conference back in April. You can’t win with zealots unless you take away the reason for the zealotry. And since it’s not really about climate and weather, but control, they were not going away. Now look at what we are seeing. The recent shift in Congress and the Senate has emboldened that extremity, so people are going to be targets. Some of those people may be held “accountable” for actions they took because they believed those actions were the best course of action. Of course, it’s not only people in the administration involved with climate and weather; it’s across the board.

I have always had a variety of clients. If a client happens to be an oil company that needs a forecast, I provide one. For instance, we have a colder December forecast than the standard strong El Niño analog. Even though December may not be cold compared to many others, it should be colder than that standard. Here is the example:
You start computing the difference in energy costs, and even though we’re by no means forecasting a frigid December — just one that’s not as warm — the difference is a big deal.

But that’s seen as taking money from an oil company. Yet wind and solar are huge items we forecast for also. So, does that put me in their pocket? Of course not. But it does to them. I found that out when I was making the Bill Nye movie as the villain. I was asked how much money I was getting from the Koch brothers because someone said they were paying me to say what I was saying. I have no idea who told them that, but I pointed to my 2007 Pontiac Firebird with a hole in the bumper and said, “How does a man getting rich off the Koch brothers drive that?” The fact is, if you did eliminate all non-wind and solar energy sources, that’s awesome for business. They need not only a seasonal forecast, but hour-by-hour forecasts. For instance, what does a 20-degree drop in a thunderstorm in Dallas do to demand? Or what if there is a prolonged heat wave in a big city, but the wind turbine source has light winds and is not producing? They need a forecast not only for an extended time period, but every day and every hour. Heck, why not just push wind and solar all the time if you are a forecaster? Now isn’t that an interesting question, as far as motivation goes? Mine is to look for trouble and forecast it, no matter who or what you are. I don’t care what your politics are. But think about this: Some people say you should care what someone’s politics are and question their profit motive. I suspect they are seeing in others what they know about themselves. In addition, there won’t be much of a profit motive anymore if the kind of draconian policies we see being touted come to pass (another leftist motivation).

articles.description: Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history, reveals Carbon Brief analysis.
paragraphs: Since 1850, the three nations – and other major fossil-fuel exporters – have exported hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 in the form of gas, oil and coal that has been burned in other countries.
Carbon Brief’s analysis of extraction-based CO2 emissions is based on figures compiled by Robbie Andrew , a senior researcher at Norwegian climate institute CICERO .
It shows that Australia is responsible for more than twice as much global warming when including emissions from its fossil-fuel exports, while Saudi Arabia has caused more than four times as much.
Australia has been under pressure for continuing to expand its fossil-fuel production ahead of the UN climate summit in Antalya, where it is co-president with host nation Turkey.

In contrast, nations that are heavily reliant on energy imports – such as Japan or Germany – are responsible for far lower shares of planet-warming emissions, if responsibility passes to fossil-fuel producers.
There are many different ways to assign historical responsibility for current global warming.
Carbon Brief has previously published analysis based on territorial emissions , the consumption of imported goods, according to colonial rule or based on historical emissions per capita.
This year is expected to be around 1.5C hotter than pre-industrial temperatures. Next year is forecast to be the hottest on record, at around 1.7C of warming.
This year-to-year variation is due to natural variability, such as El Niño . However, approximately 100% of global warming to date is the result of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.

articles.description: It is not easy being green. ‘Green’ energy has negative environmental consequences.
paragraphs: “Light pollution interrupts critical wildlife patterns for bats, migratory birds, insects (and more) and erodes biodiversity. In addition to these threats to wildlife, brighter night skies also threaten the health and natural cycles of humans, wastes energy and money, and disrupts ecosystems” according to a 2025 report from the World Economic Forum.” (- Haley Zaremba, below)

An article by Haley Zaremba (OilPrice.com) earlier this year, The Renewable Energy Transition Is Running Out of Places to Go (February 8, 2026), identified several issues of industrial wind complexes that seldom get attention. She speaks from the alarmist/transformationist camp, which makes her points extra interesting.

Just this month, a city-sized renewable energy development in Chile was scrapped after a year-long campaign led by astronomers who want to preserve the darkness of the Atacama Desert’s skies. The Atacama Desert is the highest and driest in the world, making it one of the world’s most ideal and important sites for astronomical observation. As of 2016, light pollution already covered nearly 80 percent of the planet , with a projected expansion of 2.2 percent a year . This means that a place like the Atacama is vanishingly rare. Chile’s highlands are therefore home to some of the biggest and most distinguished telescopes on the planet.

One of these, the European Southern Observatory’s (ESO’s) Paranal Observatory, would have been within five kilometers of the planned green energy site, which would occupy almost 7,500 acres (more than 3000 hectares). The ESO conducted a study on the likely impacts of this potential new neighbor and found that the megaproject would increase light pollution in the skies above the telescope by a minimum of 35 percent and increase atmospheric turbulence, further reducing clarity when observing the night sky. To nearly everyone’s surprise, the astronomers won … and the INNA (Integrated Energy Infrastructure Project for the Generation of Hydrogen and Green Ammonia) was scrapped.
“Light pollution,” Haley Zaremba concludes, “may sound like a relatively minor form of environmental degradation, but it can have serious consequences.” She explains:

Light pollution interrupts critical wildlife patterns for bats, migratory birds, insects (and more) and erodes biodiversity. In addition to these threats to wildlife, brighter night skies also threaten the health and natural cycles of humans, wastes energy and money, and disrupts ecosystems” according to a 2025 report from the World Economic Forum.

While this represents a major win for the astronomers and the sanctity of dark skies, renewable megaprojects have to go somewhere – and finding suitable sites for their construction is growing harder and harder. In developed countries, rural communities have been pushing back for years against massive-scale green energy projects in their areas, with relative success. And now, developing countries are starting to push back as well after years of bearing the brunt of these outsourced and offshored mega-developments, as well as their negative environmental and public health externalities.
articles.lede: It is not easy being green. ‘Green’ energy has negative environmental consequences.

articles.description: Unsurprisingly, the claim that heat killed 710,000 in 2023 is not based on actual data, but junk models.
paragraphs: For the tenth year running, it doubles down on the pretence that our health is suffering because of climate change and that people around the world are dropping like flies:

The past 11 years have been the hottest on record, and growing emissions mean overshooting the 1·5°C threshold is probably unavoidable—pushing the world beyond the limits needed to protect health. Indicators in this report show that, since the Paris Agreement entered into force in 2016, people have experienced not only increasing climate change-related health impacts and risks, but also an acceleration in these changes across numerous impacts compared with the previous decade. Although whether this acceleration will continue remains uncertain, it has already exacerbated adaptation challenges and claimed lives, harmed health, and affected wellbeing worldwide.

During 2016–23, heat was associated with an average of 540 800 deaths per year, of which 369 940 (68·4%) were attributable to human-caused climate change. Heat-related deaths reached a record-high of 710 000 estimated deaths globally in 2023, of which 71·5% can be attributed to climate change. Countries with a low human development index (HDI) had the highest proportion of heat-attributable deaths, reflecting the disproportionate adverse impacts of climate change on those least responsible for it, and the resulting amplification of global health inequities (indicator 1.1.5).

More frequent heatwaves and extreme droughts are increasingly threatening food security (indicator 1.4.1). Droughts affected 51·8% of global land for at least 1 month in 2025—the second-highest level recorded. This trend has accelerated, with the affected area growing 704% faster in 2016–25 than in 2006–15 (indicator 1.2.2). In parallel, the rate of increase in very extreme precipitation days, which in 2016–25 affected 17·2%% of global land annually, has also accelerated, exacerbating the risk and occurrence of health-threatening floods and landslides (indicator 1.2.3).

Rising temperatures and changing rainfall patterns have also driven an accelerated increase in the environmental suitability for dengue virus transmission, and a record-high number of people (1·72 billion) lived within 100 km of coastal waters environmentally suitable for the transmission of Vibrio bacteria in 2025 (indicators 1.3.1 and 1.3.2). Climate change is also affecting malaria and West Nile virus transmission, reducing suitability in some areas while increasing it in others (indicator 1.3.1).
All of these silly claims have been debunked year after year, so this time I will focus on:

The Lancet Countdown claims there has been a large increase in drought conditions even in just the last ten years, itself a ludicrous statement, as the world’s climate does not change measurable on such short timescales.

articles.description: The administration’s attempt to revive the declining industry is leaving workers — and the planet — behind.
paragraphs: On President Donald Trump’s watch, a quiet epidemic has been left unchecked to prey upon Appalachia’s workforce. Coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, the incurable progressive pulmonary disease better known as black lung, now affects 32% of longtime underground miners in Central Appalachia, which includes Kentucky, Virginia, and West Virginia.
That’s just one alarming statistic cited in a new report from Reimagine Appalachia, a coalition of organizations working to improve the lives of workers in Appalachia.

During Trump’s second term, his administration has taken an active role in weakening federal environmental regulations, handing over more land to mine operators, and privileging coal production over more renewable energy projects, while gutting a Biden-era rule meant to protect coal miners from black lung.

“The Trump administration has put substantive energy and funding toward expanding the coal industry without taking complementary actions to expand protections for the miners on whom the coal industry depends,” the report authors wrote.

A pet project of President Trump in his second term has been boosting what he calls “beautiful, clean coal.” The administration has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into new coal facilities, and Trump has bragged that “the United States is opening up new mines at the fastest pace since the 1950s.”

Demand for coal has continued to decline, but its extraction helps fuel climate change. As recently as 2024 , coal was responsible for almost half of all carbon dioxide emissions from U.S. electricity generation, while providing only 15% of its power. Both underground and surface coal mining operations release climate-warming methane into the atmosphere.
Meanwhile, black lung cases have increased more than 60% since 2018, to the highest rates since 1978.

For decades, coal dust presented the greatest danger to miners’ respiratory health; mine operators did little to prevent its spread, and generations of workers fell victim to the demon of the coalfields. After the passage of the 1969 Federal Coal Mine Health and Safety Act , which introduced a federal coal dust exposure limit as well as robust safety standards and engineering controls, the rate of black lung cases dropped by 90%.

In 1974, the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health recommended a stricter limit for the respirable crystalline silica that causes black lung disease. The Institute stated that miners should not be exposed to more than 50 micrograms per cubic meter during any 10-hour shift of a 40-hour work week, noting that compliance ​“should prevent adverse effects of crystalline silica.”

But the current limit, which was implemented in the 1970s, is still twice that – and that’s assuming mine operators comply. The permissible silica exposure threshold for coal miners remains double that of every other industry, including construction.
articles.lede: The administration’s attempt to revive the declining industry is leaving workers — and the planet — behind.

paragraphs: What may be the biggest item on the COP31 agenda is getting almost no press. This may be because it has no content but that is precisely the issue.
“Work programme on climate finance, including on Article 9, paragraph 1, of the Paris Agreement in the context of Article 9 of the Paris Agreement as a whole.”
What makes this very big is that Article 9, paragraph 1 is the one that says the developed countries will pay the developing countries for climate action. Here is that text:

“Developed country Parties shall provide financial resources to assist developing country Parties with respect to both mitigation and adaptation in continuation of their existing obligations under the Convention.”
“Shall” means there is a legal obligation to pay. The problem is that “assist” is vague and there is a huge difference in how the developing and developed countries interpret it.

The developing countries tend to interpret assistance as meaning the developed countries are obligated to pay for all their climate costs. Many, perhaps all, formally submitted National climate action plans are contingent on this funding.
Developed countries have treated assistance as a form of foreign aid with the amount determined by what they feel they can afford. Promises of aid may or may not be kept.

The work programme on climate finance might be tasked with trying to resolve these hugely different opposing viewpoints. Or maybe not. The actual task of the work programme is what is on the table at COP31.

The possibilities vary greatly. At one extreme the result could be naming specific annual amounts that are due from the developed countries, in effect a payment schedule that rises over time. It could even say which countries owe how much, possibly based on historic emissions. Fantasy calculations like that already exist.
At the other extreme there might just be the ever popular wished for but not enforceable targets. These numbers also already exist in various forms and amounts.
articles.lede: “Shall” means there is a legal obligation to pay. The problem is that “assist” is vague and there is a huge difference in how the developing and developed countries interpret it.

paragraphs: As seas rise and wildfires and hurricanes grow more intense, some people are asking where they could move to reduce their vulnerability.
Cincinnati is one of several northern inland cities promoting itself as a potential destination. This year, it became the first U.S. city to release a climate migration readiness plan .
Tim Robustelli is with the Future of Land and Housing program at New America, a think tank. He says an influx of new residents could bring many benefits.
Robustelli: “Economic development, entrepreneurship, and of course, with more economic activity with larger populations, that’s a larger tax base.”
But he says as Cincinnati and other cities plan to attract and support new residents, they also need to protect current residents from being left behind or pushed out.
For example, cities can provide rental assistance and create policies that protect tenants from eviction if property values rise.
Robustelli: “Other tools like property tax breaks … can sort of help offset some of the increased costs you see with redevelopment and gentrification.”
And he says grants and low-interest loans can help people pay for critical home repairs so they can stay in their homes long-term.
So cities can welcome new residents and support those who have lived there for generations.

‘Crocodiles are possible, but hunger is certain’: Malawi’s foragers forced into infested waters
articles.description: Once ‘famine food’, empty granaries have forced people along the Shire River to harvest water-lily roots in waters full of the reptiles
paragraphs: T he mid-morning heat in Malawi’s lower Shire River basin is already suffocating, but Beatrice Maseko cannot afford to look away from the water’s edge. Coated in grey, foul-smelling mud up to her thighs, the 34-year-old mother of four plunges both arms deep into the heavy sediment of a sprawling marsh. Her fingers feel blindly through the silt for the rough, bulbous roots of wild water lilies, known as nyika .

Around her, a dozen other women move with deliberate, hushed slowness. No one splashes; no one speaks above a tense whisper. Just 50 yards away, where the marsh opens into the main artery of the Shire River, the silhouette of a Nile crocodile glides silently beneath the surface.
“Every time you reach down into the mud, you wonder if your hand will come back up,” Maseko says. She spends up to five hours a day searching through these waters.

The danger is not abstract. In the villages of Maseya and neighbouring Kasisi, in southern Malawi’s Chikwawa district, people talk about foragers who have gone into the deeper channels looking for larger roots and never returned.

In 2024, Isaac Kenneth, a 28-year-old from a neighbouring settlement, was attacked while harvesting in the same stretch of water. The crocodile seized his leg and dragged him under. Fellow foragers managed to pull him free, but he suffered deep puncture wounds and a broken ankle.
“The crocodile is a possibility, but hunger is a certainty,” Maseko says, hoisting a heavy wet sack on to her shoulder. “If I do not come into this water, my children will not eat tonight.”

Nyika foraging is not new. For decades, communities in the lower Shire have harvested the tubers of the water lily ( Nymphaea petersiana ) during severe shortages, as documented in accounts from the 2005 food crisis and later lean seasons .

What has changed is the scale and regularity. Once reserved for the worst drought years, the harvest has become weekly and commercial for many families across Malawi’s flood-prone southern lowlands, as extreme weather, weak support systems and rising food prices have combined to lock vulnerable households out of basic nutrition.

Every Monday and Thursday, the tracks leading to Sorgin Market fill with vendors carrying heavy wet bundles. Women sit on colourful cloths spread over the dry earth, surrounded by plastic basins piled high with mud-encrusted lily bulbs. For buyers priced out of the maize market, one basin can mean three days of basic survival for a family. The roots are boiled, dried and pounded into a gritty grey flour used to make porridge.

articles.title: Weekly Climate and Energy News Roundup #715
articles.description: “Science knows no country, because knowledge belongs to humanity, and is the torch which illuminates the world.”— Louis Pasteur
paragraphs: Quote of the Week : “Science knows no country, because knowledge belongs to humanity, and is the torch which illuminates the world.” — Louis Pasteur

Scope : This TWTW begins with a discussion by Roy Spencer on a better way to measure the Urban Heat Island effect than population. TWTW discusses a presentation by Irish energy engineer Kieran O’Brien pointing out that the political energy mandates not only require a new system of energy generation but also a new power system which will be costly. TWTW discusses reports by the UK National Energy System Operator stating there are significant “thermal constraints” (network capacity constraints that prevent generation from reaching consumers) that are costly in the UK system. TWTW discusses an essay by David Legates on a plan to light-up your night and concludes with several announcements.
Urban Heat Island: Last week TWTW discussed Howard “Cork” Hayden’s chapter in the book Canary In a Climate World in which he states [Boldface added]:

“In 1980, if you asked a scientist about climate change, the answer would have been almost trivial. Of course, the climate changes. It always has, and it always will. Ice ages came and went, Greenland once supported Viking farms, and ecosystems shifted long before humans had any measurable influence. To say climate change is real would have been like saying water is wet.

Somewhere along the way, that simple idea was transformed into something very different. Today, climate change is no longer just a description of a changing climate. It has come to mean a problem to be controlled, and more specifically, a problem attributed largely to human activity and carbon dioxide. That shift in meaning has had profound consequences, not only for public discussion, but for how the science itself is presented.

To understand what is actually going on, it helps to step back and look at the basic physics. The Earth is governed by a simple energy balance. Energy arrives from the Sun, some of it is reflected back into space, and the rest is absorbed and eventually radiated away as heat. If more energy comes in than leaves, the planet warms. If more leaves than comes in, it cools. There are only three quantities that matter: the incoming solar radiation, the fraction reflected, known as the albedo, and the infrared radiation escaping to space.

If someone wanted to control the climate, those are the only three levers available. You could change the sunlight reaching Earth, alter how reflective the planet is by increasing clouds, ice, or atmospheric particles, or interfere with the infrared radiation leaving the planet. Everything else, storms, ocean currents, droughts, and floods, may be dramatic, but they are internal processes. They matter only to the extent that they affect one of those three quantities .”

One of the man-made internal processes that confuse many people about local and regional climate change is the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect. It is completely different than change from carbon dioxide. This well-known effect was first reported in London in 1818 and is calculated primarily by using population density. The UHI effect distorts the surface temperature record. In cities, nights are warmer than in the surrounding countryside, giving the impression that slowing of nighttime cooling is the result of greenhouse gases. Actually, buildings and pavement store daytime heat, which is slowly released at night. John Christy and Roy Spencer have produced an idea that may be better in measuring the Urban Heat Island effect – calculate the impervious surface. articles.title: Climate Change Weekly # 596—Did Climate Change Stave off the Next Ice Age? Study Says Maybe
articles.description: Research published in the journal Science suggests just that, and if true, it would mean the social cost of carbon calculations are superfluous, with the benefits outweighing the costs by a factor of thousands.
paragraphs: The Heartland Institute has long critiqued the “social cost of carbon” calculations used to monetize supposed future damages from climate change. (Consider, for example, some of our presentations at ICCC conferences , in news stories , in commentarie s, and at Climate Change Weekly ). While we and our allies have identified specific problems with the way this alleged cost is calculated, from the unrealistic models used to the woefully low discount rate, the most telling and persistent critique of the government’s modelling exercise is the failure to include any benefits from a modestly warming world to complete an honest cost-benefit comparison.

If there are, in fact, any long-term harms from climate change, a balanced, comprehensive cost-benefit analysis would almost certainly conclude the net benefits are greater than the costs. And that’s even before we consider the recent suggestion that human greenhouse gas emissions have actually staved off a coming ice age or glacial period. Research published in the journal Science suggests just that, and if true, it would mean the social cost of carbon calculations are superfluous, with the benefits outweighing the costs by a factor of thousands.

Over the last million years or so, ice ages or glaciation periods have lasted around 70,000 to 90,000 years on average, although sometimes a bit longer, and interglacial periods have been much shorter, 10,000 to 30,000 years, with most having been closer to 10,000 than 30,000. Our current interglacial cycle, the Holocene, began about 12,000 years ago, with temperatures rising abruptly and then shifting slightly up and down cyclically to the present, followed by a huge glacial retreat, with the oceans rising by fits and starts as the ice locked up in the miles-deep glaciers which covered much of the Northern Hemisphere melted and formed large and small freshwater lakes and the water flowed into the seas.

It should be obvious to all that ice ages are bad for human life and most wildlife, compressing habitat, limiting arable land, and reducing crop production. Double cropping ceases to be an option. Also, cold temperatures kill far more people than hot temperatures. As a result, an ice age would prove deadly for multiple reasons: crop production would drop sharply; mass hunger, cold-related illnesses, and premature deaths would increase sharply; and probably, with modern technologies, deadly wars for resources and living space would commence. Barring some barely imaginable technological breakthroughs, ports and coastal cities in the Northern Hemisphere would become isolated by hundreds of yards or even several miles from the nearest water, and entire cities, towns, and communities would be scraped from the surface of the Earth and covered by billions of tons of ice. We would truly have a climate immigration crisis as hundreds of millions of people from the Northern Hemisphere tried to move south.
Think “The Day After Tomorrow” but without the immediate chaos, unfolding over hundreds of years rather than across days.
articles.lede: Research published in the journal Science suggests just that, and if true, it would mean the social cost of carbon calculations are superfluous, with the benefits outweighing the costs by a factor of thousands.

articles.title: Country diary: A hard year on the farm, but I can’t help but feel optimistic
articles.description: Brigg, Lincolnshire: As I turn to the autumn jobs, loading crops and checking our machinery, I have to feel that next year will be better
paragraphs: T he days are suddenly short, and the mornings have begun to turn much colder, but – strange as it may seem – I’m feeling optimistic. This happens every year around now – I look around and see well-established winter crops full of potential, hedges and edges full of food for the wildlife, and, for now, some money back in the bank, having sold some of the harvest.

The changing colours help – not only the trees but also the yellow and the browns of the soil changing back to green. Farmers have to be the ultimate gamblers, planting a crop with no idea what price we will achieve or what yield will come. We plant and hope.

As ever, I am forever looking to the farm’s weather station. Not long ago we were desperate for rain, and there is still a deficit of moisture in the soil (we need 200mm more to hit our annual 12-year average). Rain will turn deficit into surplus; my hope then is that it doesn’t all arrive at once, as that would hit any fragile confidence I have.

You could be forgiven for thinking all is doom and gloom out here in the fields: a miserable harvest, difficult weather conditions, a lack of political will to tackle food security (we can’t just import it from abroad, grown with differing quality control standards and with chemicals long banned here). And, of course, the change in the climate isn’t about to magically go away, and we adapt to it. However, as growers we have to push forward in the belief that next year will be worth the effort. An element of optimism and resilience is our coping mechanism, a part of the job.

So for now, with all winter crops growing strongly, we start the autumnal jobs: an audit of machinery maintenance (the combine harvester won’t take long this year, as it barely broke sweat), loading the crops, assessing what went right (very little), what we could have done better (more rain in the growing season would be a start), and where we can add more life to the farm. The cycle begins again.
articles.lede: T he days are suddenly short, and the mornings have begun to turn much colder, but – strange as it may seem – I’m feeling optimistic.

articles.description: But catching the spacecraft brings SpaceX closer to a fully reusable system and makes the road to the Moon and Mars look a little less like science fiction.
paragraphs: During its 15th test flight, Starship completed 14 orbits, deployed 26 Starlink satellites, and advanced SpaceX’s push toward fully reusable spaceflight.
When we last reported on Starship, it had completed a successful attempt to orbit, which is another important step in turning Elon Musk’s ambitious plans into engineering reality.
Now the company has given space enthusiasts something truly spectacular: Starship returned from orbit and, for the first time, was caught by the giant “Mechazilla” arms at its Texas launch tower.

After a 22-hour stay in space, a SpaceX Starship rocket plunged back to Earth Saturday, enduring the blazing heat of reentry while homing in on its Texas Gulf Coast launch site, flipping vertical at the last moment and settling into the grasp of two huge mechanical arms on its launch gantry.

Throngs of SpaceX employees gathered nearby cheered and applauded as the rocket restarted three of its six methane-fueled Raptor engines to flip upright, rapidly slowing to a near hover as the robot arms moved in for a mechanical embrace, catching the rocket a moment before engine shutdown.

…It was the first such recovery of a Starship from orbit — previous test flights ended with planned ocean splashdowns — marking a major milestone in SpaceX’s drive to develop the first fully reusable orbit-class rocket, a vehicle company founder Elon Musk says will dramatically lower the cost of launching payloads to Earth orbit, the moon and, eventually, Mars.

The Starship was launched atop a Super Heavy booster Friday using the same pad at SpaceX’s Starbase facility on the Texas coast. Standing 407 feet tall, the two-stage rocket is the most powerful launcher ever built, generating some 16 million pounds of thrust at liftoff from 33 first-stage Raptor engines.

SpaceX originally planned to catch Super Heavy with the Starbase launch tower’s giant mechanical “chopstick” arms. But it wasn’t to be: The company called off the catch attempt and brought the booster down for a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after launch, for reasons that were not immediately clear.

A successful catch would have been a significant milestone for SpaceX and its efforts to design Starship as a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle. It would have been the first successful recovery of a Version 3 (V3) Super Heavy, which SpaceX began flying earlier this year. The company previously recovered three of its V1 Super Heavy vehicles and reused two of those in later flights.
But catching the spacecraft brings SpaceX closer to a fully reusable system and makes the road to the Moon and Mars look a little less like science fiction.

paragraphs: Researchers find little evidence of widespread waste-heat-driven surface warming around data center clusters near Tokyo.

In my last post on data centers , I noted that an urban environmental activist, paired with a group sponsored by a billionaire Marxist linked to China, promoted a campaign to generate so much fear and loathing of a data center project that local residents rejected it.

As I reported in “ Voters Pull the Plug on Big Tech’s AI Data Center Boom ,” voters across the country embraced restrictions on these projects, raising the troubling possibility that this Maryland saga is one chapter in a much larger story, and this pairing of anti-American NGOs with activists is detrimental to our nation’s development of artificial intelligence (AI).
Part of the environmental campaign against data centers has been that they contribute to “global warming” and that they create urban “heat islands”, as noted by The Weather Channel .

A new global study found that the data centers powering artificial intelligence are doing more than consuming massive amounts of electricity and water. Turns out they might also be significantly warming the land around them.
This is creating localized “heat islands” that affect hundreds of millions of people, say researchers.

The vast data centers that power artificial intelligence guzzle huge amounts of energy but they also have another alarming impact, according to new research. They are creating “ heat islands ,” warming the land around them by up to 16 degrees Fahrenheit, and making life hotter for more than 340 million people.

However, a new study refutes this effect, arguing that the reflective surfaces associated with data center construction help lower localized temperatures. In the article (“Satellite observations and energy balance constrain the thermal footprint of a hyperscale data-centre cluster,”), sole author Jiawei Jing of Makuhari Development Corporation uses satellite measurements and energy-balance calculations to find little evidence of widespread waste-heat-driven surface warming around data center clusters near Tokyo.

Published in Environmental Research Letters , Jing’s study uses satellite observations, comparison sites, construction timelines, and calculations to determine how much warming their electricity consumption could support.

The analysis covers twelve facilities commissioned between 2011 and 2025, although its strongest comparison centers on one facility with clearly separated construction and operating periods. A second cluster provides checks.

articles.title: Unusually Low Pressure Caused Sea Level to Rise
articles.description: Thus, sea level over Seattle was elevated by 27 cm or 10.6 inches by the low pressure. Almost a foot!
paragraphs: Consider a plot of sea-level pressure for SeaTac Airport since July (below). The pressure dropped to 990 hPa, the lowest observed during the period, by a LOT.

Our extremely low pressure was associated with a deep low-pressure center immediately to our west (see the analysis at 4 AM Friday). At this time, the low center had a central pressure of 968 hPa, which is low for this latitude.
The average pressure for Seattle in November is 1017 hPa (the average around the nation is 1013 hPa), so our pressure on Friday was 27 hPa below normal.
Localized low pressure causes sea level to rise by approximately 1 cm for every decline of 1 hPa. (See schematic below).
Thus, sea level over Seattle was elevated by 27 cm or 10.6 inches by the low pressure. Almost a foot!

Below is a plot below of predicted (blue) versus observed (red) sea level in Seattle. The difference between the two has increased this week as the low-pressure center approached, with sea level 2.2 feet above normal.

The low center is associated with powerful westerly (from the west) and southwesterly winds (see forecast surface winds at 1 PM Friday below). Winds near the coast were strongly from the south (southerly)

Such southerly winds push on the ocean surface, which flows TOWARDS the coast by the Coriolis force, resulting in a HIGHER water level. See schematic below of this situation. Want to impress your friends? This is called Ekman Transport .
The offshore low with strong winds over a large area (long fetch) produces big waves that can bring the water levels up even more on the coast (see forecast wave heights for Friday morning below).
There are other, more minor contributors to short-term high water levels, such as a Kelvin wave associated with the El Nino moving up the coast (several inches).

articles.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: the green transition must not be derailed
articles.description: Editorial: Renewed commitments to electrification and climate science are vital outcomes from the latest round of UN talks
paragraphs: T he Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the US midterms means that Donald Trump’s destructive grip has been loosened. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34.

While the diplomatic picture is less bleak than it might have been, the threat level remains high and rising. António Guterres used his last Cop as UN secretary general to issue a pithy warning that “ it’s make or bake time ”. With the latest analysis pointing to heating of 2.7C by the end of the century – far beyond the 1.5C target in the Paris agreement – governments face another crunch moment: by pivoting away from fossil fuels, they can still avert the most dangerous impacts. Yet the UK’s Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to make the trip to Turkey; the French and German leaders chose to attend an EU summit in Dublin instead.

Warnings of mounting risks, unprecedented heat and disasters such as August’s glacier collapse on the Nepal-Tibet border can engender a sense of paralysis or unreality. The leaders of both host countries prompted anger last week: the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, publicly extolled his country’s oil reserves , while Australia’s Anthony Albanese failed to mention fossil fuels in his speech. But for all its flaws, the UN climate process remains crucial. There is no other mechanism to broker a global green transition.

Mr Burnham’s appointment of a climate security adviser , Madeleine Alessandri, should focus minds in the UK. Kemi Badenoch’s rejection of net zero has undermined an important cross‑party consensus. Ministers, who must soon make a decision on Rosebank oil and gas field , must realise that economic damage caused by the carbon pollution from the oil and gas produced would dwarf any benefits. Governments of countries that are far poorer than the UK cannot be expected to turn away from coal and oil if rich countries keep investing.

A resolution to derive 35% of energy worldwide from electricity by 2035 will be agreed this week if objections from fossil fuel producers can be overcome. Attempts to undermine the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change must also be resisted. It provides the science on which the process depends. Increased accountability on climate finance is urgently needed too. Poor countries cannot be expected to put up with endless delays .

A large majority of the global public recognises the threat from global heating and wants action by governments. Of course, this takes courage and leadership: people may back a green transition in the abstract, but be more resistant to changes that affect their lives. But those pushing for a faster shift away from fossil fuels, at Cop31 and at a national level, should be emboldened by the way that public awareness and support have grown: they are on the side of the future, while their opponents are stuck in the past.
articles.lede: T he Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space.

paragraphs: Human-caused climate change could increase flood damage to commercial property in parts of Europe by as much as 800% over the next 30 years compared to the period 1990-2016, according to a recent paper published by the UK Met Office. The paper’s findings are aimed at pension fund investors so they can “better understand” the risks in a changing climate. In fact, the findings belong in clown land since they are all based on the assumptions fed into climate computer models known as RCP8.5. Earlier this year, RCP8.5 was declared “implausible” by a sub-committee of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) that was preparing groundwork for a major new assessment report.

Implausible Day was April 7th 2026, and quite why the Met Office continues to use this garbage in, garbage out computer model scenario is a complete mystery. RCP8.5 became the normal basis for many media clickbait scare headlines over the last 15 years, and it was ruthlessly used to back the political Net Zero fantasy. Even activist scientists must now realise that with its fanciful assumptions of runaway population growth and coal-use higher than known reserves, it is a busted flush. All it seems except the blinkers-wearing boffins at the bumbling British Met Office.

Its latest paper is called ‘Assessing financial risk to property portfolios from physical rainfall extremes’. And where do the Met Office authors get estimates for “extreme” rainfall? Surprise, surprise, another Met Office work called UK Climate Projections (UKCP18) that only used a RCP8.5 computer run to claim summer temperature in the UK would be 5°C higher by 2070, while rainfall would be much lower in the warmer months and considerably higher in the winter. Excellent Net Zero messaging here of course, with future drought and flooding helping to scare everyone witless. Needless to say, the ghastly UKCP18 report should have been withdrawn last April, preferably with a fulsome apology for all the trouble it has caused with its whacky forecasts. Of course it wasn’t, and its pathetic presence is still stinking up the science joint.

The new Met Office research examines flood risk across north-east Europe, covering the UK, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark, parts of France, Germany, the Czech Republic, Poland, Norway and Sweden. The findings from the 1990-2016 baseline are striking. Across the study region, the authors claim that there will be widespread increases in annual damage with only 0.1% of locations showing no change. Many areas showed increases exceeding 20%, while some individual 100-metre grid cells claimed rises of up to 800%. The authors specifically identified central London, Hamburg and Odense as areas where guesstimated flood damage was particularly pronounced.

The authors claim their findings “highlight the urgent need for financial actors, such as asset managers, to integrate physical climate risk into decision-making to safeguard long-term financial resilience”. Who knows what this waffle means, but indications elsewhere in the report suggest, as with most matters Net Zero, the dishing out loads of dosh at a problem juiced up by junk computer findings.

New Study: Barents Sea Temperatures Were Warmer And Sea Ice Less Extensive In The 1700s Than Today
articles.description: These proxy records demonstrate that reduced sea-ice conditions are not exclusive to the modern era.
paragraphs: In a 2026 study published in Communications Earth & Environment , scientists have analyzed marine sediment cores (NPAL04, BASICC 1, and BASICC 43) from the northern Barents Sea to reconstruct historical sea-ice conditions and marine productivity.

Using highly branched isoprenoid (HBI) diatom biomarkers—specifically HBI III and HBI IV as well as EZ₂₅ sea surface temperature (SST) proxy—the researchers mapped ocean temperatures across recent centuries.

As illustrated in the study’s multi-core comparison, the EZ₂₅ SST records (shown in yellow) indicate that sea surface temperatures in the Barents Sea were warmer during the 1700s than they were in the 2000s.

Alongside these temperature trends, the researchers examined historical sea-ice coverage using spring sea ice (SpSIC) reconstructions and the sea-ice biomarker IP₂₅ (shown in blue). These proxy records demonstrate that reduced sea-ice conditions are not exclusive to the modern era.

Across the Barents Sea cores, spring sea-ice presence was just as low—or even lower—than 2000s levels during several distinct historical intervals, including the 1700s, the 1800s, and the mid-twentieth century from the 1930s to the 1950s.
articles.lede: These proxy records demonstrate that reduced sea-ice conditions are not exclusive to the modern era.

articles.description: So, while the UHI effect in NYC is quite large (+3 to +4 deg. C (+5.4 to +7.2 deg. F) at several GHCN stations), since 1985 the increase in UHI has been rather weak, at least using the small increases in impervious surface area coverage as a proxy for increased urbanization.
paragraphs: John Christy and I just submitted a paper for publication in the AMS Journal of Applied Meteorology and Climatology called “ Average Summer Heat Island Effects Relative to Landsat Impervious Surface Area for 50 Major U.S. Cities, 1985-2025 “. You can tell what it’s about from the title.

As you might recall, a couple of years ago we published a paper relating GHCN station air temperatures to population density, and I made maps of the global distributions of UHI warming based upon those calculations.

But population density is not the best choice as a proxy for urbanization when it comes to the urban heat island (UHI) effect. The reason I used it is that there are global gridpoint datasets of population density going back to at least 1800, and how much UHI warming there has been in cities should be compared to what temperatures would be if the city was not there. The very first published study of the UHI effect was in 1818 by Luke Howard for London.

So, a couple years ago, I started a new analysis using Landsat satellite-based impervious surface area (ISA), which should be the single most direct physical influence on UHI warming. ISA measures the spatial coverage (in percent) of roads, parking lots, roofs, and many more types of human-built structures and modified soil surfaces (e.g. railways). The spatial resolution is 30×30 meters, and the dataset begins in 1985, now updated through 2025.

I analyzed all of the June, July, and August GHCN station data within 30 to 100 km of the center of the 50 most populous Metropolitan Statistical Areas (MSAs) used by the U.S. Census Bureau. The following image shows those station locations.

This was a tedious, time-consuming process, partly because I also wanted to see if the UHI effect was magnified in these cities during excessively hot weather (warmer than the 97th percentile threshold temperature in Tmax). Determining that threshold from many stations in each of the 50 MSAs (which averaged 27 stations) was not straightforward.

I also simplified the methodology compared to our previous population-density related work: the example plots that follow are based upon how much each GHCN station’s daily Tmax or Tmin temperature departs from the average of all stations within the MSA (rural, suburban, and urban). This is basically what many of us experience on a daily basis as we commute from more rural locations to more urban locations, or drive across the city. Those individual station departures from the MSA-wide multi-station averages were then related to the impervious surface area centered on that GHCN station at 7 different averaging spatial resolutions (from 30×30 m to 10×10 km). The ISA averaging resolution producing the greatest magnitude correlation (positive or negative) was then chosen for further analysis.

It was quite a coincidence that two of the most extreme, and yet somewhat opposite, examples came from the two most populous MSAs: New York City and Los Angeles. The following plot shows how the New York City MSA GHCN station temperatures related to their impervious surface area.

articles.description: There is no financial incentive for building new gas plants, which will be on idle for most of the time and which will be banned eventually because of Net Zero.
paragraphs: In the past seven days we have been getting 61% of our electricity from gas, plus another 9% from burning trees:
As I repeatedly point out, it does not matter how many wind farms you build, three times nothing is still nothing!
Timera published this chart the other day, showing that 15 GW of CCGT capacity is at risk of retirement in the next 10 years because of age:
There is no financial incentive for building new gas plants, which will be on idle for most of the time and which will be banned eventually because of Net Zero.
Miliband’s answer was gas plants fitted with carbon capture, but so far only one has been given a contract – Net Zero Teesside Power, with capacity of 742 MW.

Much of his £22bn bung to carbon capture will be spent on the storage and transport of CO2, rather than the generation plants. BEIS levelised costs imply that CAPEX and OPEX for CCGT with Carbon Capture would add £2.2bn to the cost of a conventional CCGT over its lifetime, excluding interest costs.

It is therefore unlikely the budget will be enough to cover more than a handful of plants – Timera have estimated 9GW by 2040 in their modelling, but this is probably hopelessly overoptimistic. At the least, it is highly unlikely this capacity could be constructed and connected to carbon storing sites by then.
Which brings us back to the initial question. How will the grid cope if a large chunk of its CCGT capacity disappears in the next ten years?

paragraphs: MIA Is there anyone in the cockpit? A week into COP31 and there’s a definite sense of drift. The co-hosts are lying low, work on a main political/cover text seems a mess (even containing reference to the “ largely defunct ” Kyoto Protocol) and levels of support for the 35% by 2035 electrification deal are a mystery. Silence is not unusual but it’s a little worrying. Maybe they’ve been learning a new dance ( like this ). Choreography next week is key. Wrap Saturday usually sees a marked shift in gear at COPs as ministers arrive and the main negotiating venues of week 1 (SBI & SBSTA) formally close. UN climate boss Simon ‘no silver bullet’ Stiell’s 10:30 presser and the 13:00 Presidency briefing will offer a vibe check. It’s unclear if we’ll see fireworks or everyone exude hammam chill in plenary sessions as envoys debate adaptation finance, 1.5C overshoot, GST2 and the IPCC. Bonus We made it through Friday 13th without the world reaching infinity population, as predicted by the journal Science back in 1960. Turns out Australia PM Albanese and his environment minister/COP co-boss Bowen have a theory why that’s the case. The pair were caught live on air discussing the danger of phone radiation on their penises . “My d**k, that’s rather important, arguably more important than the heart,” said Bowen.

Socks Beware COPs bearing gifts. In 2015 at the Paris Agreement the media got a tote bag. In 2021 in Glasgow it was a can of Irn-Bru and a deep fried pizza. In 2026 the bribes - sorry gifts - are next level. Bags, bottles, laptop stands, magnets, lapel pins, cuddly toys and two pairs of socks, which hopefully isn’t a sign we’re going to run over next weekend. We asked our Turkish colleague and he promised the power bank probably won't be bugged. Bookmarks *IEA: Energy crisis policy tracker *Carbon Brief: Who wants what at COP31? *Carbon Brief: Negotiating text tracker *NRDC: International climate finance tracker *CAT: GHG analysis of all major emitters *ENB: Priceless daily update from inside the talks Sitrep So where are we as week 1 wraps? Here’s our traffic-light take. COP veterans won’t be shocked that we’re mostly on red, amber at best. 1. Is finance allocated by COP31 to Nepal for reconstruction/early warning ? 2. Is there a clean electrification goal ? Does it include $$$, grids & policies? 3. Are new fossil fuel phaseout plans published by governments? 4. Will hosts Türkiye & Australia commit to curbing coal use/exports ? 5. Is there an agreed plan to triple adaptation finance (as agreed in 2025)? 6. Have countries agreed (in negotiations) on how Global Stocktake 2 will work? 7. Will the IPCC deliver its next blockbuster report by GST2/2028?

We mulled over what song would be totally out of keeping with the last week, and Lindsay chose her favourite tune of all time: ‘Tubthumping’ by Chumbawunba . Comments as ever to Lindsay.smith@gsccnetwork.org .

And now, ironworkers are also essential for building another kind of tall tower – wind turbines.
Noah Mihaly, a union ironworker for White Construction, is helping build the Coles Wind Farm in Illinois.
Mihaly: “It’s almost entirely ironworkers that are preparing the engine rooms, preparing the blades … and then putting together all the pieces, as well as constructing the foundations.”
Given their vital role in building wind farms, ironworkers are in high demand as the clean energy industry expands.
So to recruit and prepare more people for these jobs, Illinois established a workforce training program under the state’s Climate and Equitable Jobs Act.
Called the Climate Works Pre-Apprenticeship Program, it provides people from underserved areas with free training and help applying to apprenticeships.

GST: What/why/when The Global Stocktake takes place every 5 years. The first was at COP28 (2023), the second will be at COP33 (2028). ¿Se puede recoger agua de lluvia en Estados Unidos?
articles.description: Yale Climate Connections is a nonpartisan, multimedia service providing daily broadcast radio programming and original web-based reporting, commentary, and analysis on the issue of climate change.
paragraphs: En el jardín de Mario Ríos, el cambio se notó primero en las orquídeas. Después de analizar el agua de pozo que utilizaba para regar y descubrir que presentaba intrusión de sodio, este residente del condado de Broward, en el sur de Florida, decidió instalar dos barriles para recoger la lluvia. “Después de comenzar a usar el agua de lluvia, vi una gran diferencia en la salud de mis plantas, especialmente de mis orquídeas”, relató.

Ríos obtuvo los depósitos después de completar una clase sobre el uso y la instalación de barriles de lluvia. El Programa de Voluntarios Master Gardener de la Universidad de Florida enseña jardinería a personas que luego, como voluntarias, educan a la comunidad de Broward County. La capacitación busca que las personas que reciben los barriles sepan cómo utilizarlos y puedan instalarlos conectados a las canaletas o colocarlos al aire libre. Al terminarla, Ríos pudo obtener sus dos barriles mediante el programa local. “Cada barril almacena 55 galones de agua de lluvia”, explicó. En conjunto, pueden guardar hasta 110 galones para regar sus plantas.

La experiencia de Ríos muestra, a escala doméstica, el potencial de esta práctica ante un clima marcado por lluvias extremas y períodos secos que presionan el abastecimiento de agua. La Quinta Evaluación Nacional del Clima de Estados Unidos, publicada en 2023, indica que, entre 1958 y 2021, la cantidad total de precipitación caída durante el 1 % de los días más lluviosos aumentó 60 % en el noreste y 45 % en el medio oeste, las dos regiones con los mayores incrementos del país. Sin embargo, el potencial de la cosecha de lluvia y las normas que la regulan varían de un estado a otro.

El cambio climático contribuye a intensificar este fenómeno. A medida que aumentan las temperaturas, se intensifica la evaporación, lo que incrementa la humedad disponible en la atmósfera y puede alimentar tormentas con precipitaciones más fuertes. Según l a Agencia de Protección Ambiental de Estados Unidos, el calentamiento causado por las actividades humanas ha contribuido al aumento de estos episodios en el país.

Sin embargo, recibir una gran cantidad de lluvia en pocas horas no significa que el agua estará disponible cuando se necesite. El sur de Florida vivió un ejemplo reciente de ese contraste: después de varios meses de sequía, el 26 de octubre de 2025 cayeron hasta 10 pulgadas de lluvia en apenas tres horas en el noreste de Broward y el sureste de Palm Beach. Las precipitaciones inundaron viviendas, dejaron más de 100 vehículos varados y generaron decenas de llamadas de rescate. Según el Servicio Meteorológico Nacional, las lluvias de finales de octubre de 2025 pusieron fin temporalmente a la sequía en la región, pero las condiciones de sequía moderada regresaron a mediados de noviembre del mismo año.

articles.title: October 2026: Earth’s warmest October on record
articles.description: The year 2026 is expected to be Earth's 2nd-warmest year on record, with 2027 likely to be the warmest.
paragraphs: October 2026 was the planet’s warmest October since modern record-keeping began in 1850, NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information , or NCEI, reported on November 12. NASA and the European Copernicus Climate Change Service also rated it as the warmest October. The global average temperature for January-October 2026 was the second-highest on record, trailing only 2024.

Global ocean surface temperatures set their fifth consecutive monthly record in October, and the month produced the highest departure from ocean-temperature average for any month in 177 years of analysis. Global land temperatures were the third highest on record for any October. It was the third-warmest October on record for global temperatures estimated by satellite through the lowest few miles of the atmosphere (the lower troposphere).

According to the European Copernicus Climate Change Service , 2026 will most likely be the second-warmest year on record (about 80% probability), with about a 20% chance of tying or exceeding 2024 as the warmest year on record. Climate scientist Zeke Hausfather and NASA both project that 2026 will be the first or second-warmest year on record, behind 2024, with 2027 likely to run away with the record. (Strong El Niño events normally peak in northern winter, and global temperature is typically higher in the second calendar year of the event than in the first one because of El Niño’s massive release of heat from ocean to atmosphere.)

The 48 contiguous United States racked up the fourth-warmest average temperature for any U.S. October in data going back to 1895, behind only 1963, 2024, and 1947. The nation’s year-to-date average temperature (Jan.-Oct.) was easily the warmest on record (see the Bluesky posts by climatologist Brian Brettschneider below). Unless the Nov.-Dec. period is substantially colder than the average from recent decades, the calendar year 2026 will end up as the warmest in U.S. history ( see our writeup from Nov. 9 ).

An El Niño advisory continues in the Eastern Pacific, NOAA reported in its November 12 monthly discussion of the state of the El Niño/Southern Oscillation, or ENSO. Sea surface temperatures in the benchmark Niño 3.4 region for the period August-September-October (the Oceanic Niño Index, or ONI) were at 2.5°C above average , the first time on record that the Aug.-Oct. value has been above 2°C. The monthly anomaly for October exceeded 3°C, as shown in the Bluesky graphic embedded below.

NOAA’s newer Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI), which adjusts the three-month value based on warmth throughout the global tropics, was at +2.0°C for Aug.-Oct. 2026, slightly below the record-setting +2.1°C from Aug.-Oct. 1997. Whether we use ONI or RONI, we have already reached the threshold of 2.0°C above average that is used to define “super” (i.e., very strong) El Niño conditions. See our writeup from November 11 on more on these indices and on how this El Niño event may shape the coming winter across the U.S. Gulf Coast and East Coast states.

articles.description: UK foreign secretary and COP veteran Ed Miliband in Antalya spoke with Carbon Brief earlier today at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, to answer readers’ questions.
paragraphs: UK foreign secretary and COP veteran Ed Miliband spoke with Carbon Brief earlier today at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, to answer readers’ questions.

Carbon Brief readers submitted questions via CB Connect on topics including the UK’s “climate leadership”, the COP31 electrification target, as well as the roadmaps on deforestation and fossil fuels .
Despite recent criticism over the approval of the Jackdaw gas field, Miliband argued that the UK is still seen as a climate leader, due to its “ambitious targets on net-zero”.
Pushing back on a question about COP reform, Miliband explained how he is “quite pro the institution of the COP”, given its role in bringing countries together for climate action.
He emphasised the importance of action on methane and the UK’s “support” for the “35×35” electrification pledge .
Carbon Brief: Well, thanks very much for joining us. I know you’re very busy and we’ve got some reader questions. It’s great that you’ve got time to answer some.
CB: How, in your experience at COP31 so far, has the UK’s decision to approve the Jackdaw gas field and the rumoured rollback of its EV targets affected the UK’s standing as a climate leader?

EM: People see us as showing leadership. People don’t see us as rolling back, and I think what people see is a government that is driving the agenda on electrification and clean power. Because after all, we have a clean power 2030 target, which is world-leading.
[We] have the most ambitious targets on net-zero, the [ nationally determined contributions ] NDCs, of frankly, any country in the world. [We] are legislating for no new oil and gas licences.

And what I’m trying to do here is also bring a new dimension to this, which is the whole national security dimension. Because I think, if you’re serious about national security, you need to be serious about climate. And those parties – and those people – who aren’t serious about climate, I don’t think they’re serious about national security. Because this is a national security issue for, I think – frankly – every government across the world.

Heading into COP31 amid geopolitical uncertainty, most delegates arrived in Antalya with the comfort of one near-certainty: the summit would produce a cover decision, the overarching text that carries its high-level political message.
But in the first rounds of consultations this week, a group made up mainly of large emerging economies has made it clear to the hosts that this is far from a done deal.

Russia, Saudi Arabia and the Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDCs), a group that includes India and China, have repeatedly questioned the legitimacy of the process proposed by Australia and cast doubt on whether a cover decision is needed at all, according to sources familiar with the discussions.

Türkiye's Zero Waste initiative - which is a vague plan to reduce waste generation and increase recycling, rather than a specific goal to reach zero waste by any specific date - was launched in 2017.
