articles.title: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31
articles.description: The amount of public funding pledged to help developing countries tackle climate change has dropped by more than 70% in 2026, according to Carbon Brief analysis.
paragraphs: Developed countries are required under UN climate treaties to provide “ climate finance ” and have traditionally announced multi-year pledges to feed into their global commitments.
Most of these pledges expired in 2025 and, since then, the US has withdrawn from international climate efforts and many European aid budgets have been cut.
A civil-society tracker shows that only six nations have announced new multi-year pledges, including just one major donor – the UK.
Germany, France and Japan are among the key contributors that have so far failed to set out plans for new climate finance, while none is expected from the US.
Experts tell Carbon Brief that global conflict, fiscal constraints and the rise of the far right are all making it harder for developed-country governments to pledge new funds.
As the COP31 summit in Turkey gets underway, developing countries are stressing their urgent need for new finance, after nations agreed to a new global target just two years ago.
Under the Paris Agreement , developed countries are obliged to provide climate finance to help developing countries cut their emissions and prepare for climate disasters.
This financial assistance can be channelled through multilateral development banks , UN climate funds and investments “mobilised” from the private sector.

But a large chunk is also expected to come directly from the public coffers of developed countries – primarily their foreign-aid budgets. This public spending has made up roughly a third of climate finance flowing to developing countries in recent years.

articles.description: More than 92,000 people have registered to attend the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, potentially making it the largest COP in history.
paragraphs: Carbon Brief analysis of the provisional lists of delegates, published by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), reveals that more than 14,000 delegates have been registered as “host country guests”.
For comparison, the final list for COP30 in Belém, Brazil, last year included only around 1,300 delegates in this category.
As with COP30 , Donald Trump’s US government has not sent a delegation. Other no-shows include Israel and Myanmar.

It was reported ahead of the summit that Taliban officials from Afghanistan had been registered for the event as observers; however, there are no delegates from observer states in the provisional lists.
With more than 3,000 “virtual” delegates signed up to attend the summit online, the total number of people registered for the event surpasses 95,000.

Pacific Island ministers also recently announced their intention to develop a regional roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels. articles.description: Repayments on climate loans could overtake new lending by 2036, according to CARE analysis shared exclusively with Climate Home News
paragraphs: With rich governments and development banks delivering more climate finance as loans, developing countries could be paying back more each year than they receive in new lending by the mid-2030s, new research has found.

CARE Denmark and the CARE Climate Justice Center worked out the repayment schedules of around 17,500 climate loan records reported by developed countries and multilateral lenders between 2011 and 2024, in what the researchers say is the first analysis of its kind.

With rich governments and development banks delivering more climate finance as loans, developing countries could be paying back more each year than they receive in new lending by the mid-2030s, new research has found.

CARE Denmark and the CARE Climate Justice Center worked out the repayment schedules of around 17,500 climate loan records reported by developed countries and multilateral lenders between 2011 and 2024, in what the researchers say is the first analysis of its kind.
If climate lending stays at its 2024 level each year and on the same terms, annual repayments on old and new loans would overtake fresh lending in 2036, the researchers found.

articles.title: Fossil-fuel CO2 emissions set to dip in 2026 as Iran conflict hits oil use
articles.description: Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels and cement are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2bn…
paragraphs: Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels and cement are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 (GtCO2), according to new figures from the Global Carbon Project .

The 21st edition of the annual “global carbon budget” report, published today , says that this small decline is largely due to a 1.9% drop in emissions from oil and the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict and the closure of the strait of Hormuz.
The Global Carbon Project’s projections for fossil fuel and cement CO2 emissions in 2026 are preliminary, with a range that spans a fall of -1.5% to a rise of +0.6%.
This is primarily driven by peat fires and forest degradation in south-east Asia and is linked to the development of a strong El Niño event this year.
As a result, total CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and land use are projected to reach a record high of 43.3GtCO2 in 2026 – marginally above 42.8GtCO2 in 2025.

Research published alongside the report by the same team in Nature Climate Change finds that the growth in solar, wind and electric vehicles (EVs) now offsets around two-thirds of the emissions that would otherwise come from rising energy demand.
However, the deployment of these technologies is not yet enough to push global emissions into a sustained decline, according to the study.
(For more on previous editions of the Global Carbon Project’s annual report, see Carbon Brief’s coverage in 2025 , 2024 , 2023 and 2022 .)
Total global CO2 emissions, which combines fossil fuels and land-use change, are projected to reach a record high of 43.3GtCO2 in 2026, up from 42.8GtCO2 in 2025.
The increase in 2026 comes entirely from a projected rise in land-use emissions, which are more challenging to estimate than fossil emissions.

Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’?
articles.description: Carbon Brief looks at where the idea for the BAM came from, how it could support just transitions and what to expect from COP31
paragraphs: One of the key expected outcomes from the upcoming COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is the launch of a “just transition mechanism”.
This follows years of calls from civil society to support a “ just transition ” as countries shift towards low-emissions energy systems and away from fossil fuels.
At the COP30 UN climate talks last year in the Brazilian city of Belém parties agreed to establish a “mechanism” to support this goal, called the “Belém-Antalya mechanism” (BAM).
Groups that have championed the BAM want it to act as a central hub on just transitions, providing support for workers and communities around the world.
However, the details of exactly what the much-touted BAM will consist of remain vague, with developed and developing countries disagreeing about its functions and purpose.
Disagreements continued at the UN climate talks in Bonn in June 2026, including on the crucial question of how the BAM will be financed.
Here, Carbon Brief looks at where the idea for the BAM came from, how it could support just transitions and what to expect from COP31.
A “ just transition ” is the idea that workers and communities should be supported in the shift to a low-carbon economy. It is a central principle behind the idea of climate justice .
Often, the term refers to those linked to the fossil-fuel industry, but it can also refer to transitions taking place in agriculture , heavy industry and various other sectors.
The concept originated in the 1980s, when US labour unions forged alliances with environmental justice groups. It has since become a key part of international climate discussions.

articles.title: Climate Diplomacy Brief
articles.description: 100,000 expected in Antalya as annual UN climate summit opens amid bubbling geopolitical tensions
paragraphs: Use your illusion A city with hotels modelled on the Kremlin, Concorde, Chrysler building and Titanic was always destined to host a UN climate summit. The annual COP is filled with KGB intrigue, sonic-boom-breaking expectations, sky-high aspirations and diplomatic icebergs. Antalya has seen off the Greek, Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman Empires. Late nights and acronyms may yet break it. Let’s COP!

Context COP1 kicked off in 1995. Angela Merkel was the future. 31 years on, many of the warnings from scientists are now coming true. Record greenhouse gas emissions are spiking global temperatures. Glaciers are crumbling. Oceans are broiling. A super El Niño is lurking. Outgoing UN chief Guterres is rumbling. “We can no longer have endless discussions in which everybody tries to push the responsibility to someone else,” he told AP.

Expectations “No single COP is a silver bullet that can stop climate change overnight” is the new favourite line of UN climate chief Stiell. Serious expectations management are afoot. Türkiye is placing emphasis on the voluntary ‘Action Agenda’. Australia is talking up ‘practical action’. The geopolitics are tortuous, but don’t head to the Kremlin waterpark just yet. Soaring oil & gas prices and cleantech’s growth offer a little more hope, as IEA boss Birol details here.

Benchmarks “COP31 lacks a single ‘big-ticket’ mandate – it is a classic intermediate COP,” writes veteran French climate diplomat Paul Watkinson. He’s probably right, but with AFP reporting 100,000 are expected to attend it does need to deliver some tickets, otherwise why bother? Below are the benchmarks we’re working with:

1. Is finance allocated by COP31 to Nepal for reconstruction/early warning? 2. Is there a clean electrification goal? Does it include $$$, grids & policies? 3. Are new fossil fuel phaseout plans published by governments? 4. Will hosts Türkiye & Australia commit to curbing coal use/exports? 5. Is there a plan to triple adaptation finance (as agreed in 2025)? 6. Have countries agreed (in negotiations) on how Global Stocktake 2 will work? 7. Will the IPCC deliver its next blockbuster report by GST2/2028?

Bedfellows They should get on: in many respects Australia and Türkiye are similar climate and energy beasts. Both have climate plans ranked pretty rubbish by Climate Action Tracker. Both love coal. Both also love solar and want to protect the ocean. One key difference is while Kurum is happy to discuss moving away from fossil fuels, Bowen is evidently under orders from above not to mention Australia’s addiction, which as negotiations lead is a little awkward.

Tuesday evening’s consultations/ bushtucker trial will be a test for the Oz/Turk relationship. Do they push for a Christmas tree text (shiny, baubles, lacking substance) or stay focused on clean electrification and fossil fuels, tripling adaptation finance etc? It’s a choice.

articles.title: ‘Simply staggering’: Rapidly developing ‘super El Niño’ on track to peak in December
articles.description: The ongoing “super El Niño” is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to record levels next year.
paragraphs: That is according to Carbon Brief’s latest “ state of the climate ” update, which analyses El Niño forecasts from more than a dozen climate models, as well as six global temperature datasets. Dr Zeke Hausfather , Carbon Brief’s climate science contributor, described this year’s El Niño as “simply staggering” when answering questions from CB+ members during a CB Connect “ ask me anything ” session.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific that releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere and temporarily boosts global temperatures.

This year’s El Niño event – which has been underway since June – has already broken a number of records and reshaped the world’s weather, fuelling fires in Indonesia and “super typhoons” in the west Pacific.
The strength of an El Niño is tracked using the “Niño3.4 anomaly”, which is a measure of how much warmer sea surface temperatures are than average in a section of the central Pacific.

Analysis of more than 600 forecasts from 14 different climate models by Hausfather for Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” update shows how models project this year’s El Niño will peak with an anomaly of around 4C. This would be more than a degree above the previous record in 2015-16.

“This El Niño event is developing so quickly and is reaching sea surface temperatures so warm that it’s simply staggering. We haven’t seen anything like this in the historical record and it may end up being the strongest El Niño event in the past millennium.”
On 18 September, the daily anomaly in the Niño3.4 region broke the satellite-era record set in 2015 when it reached 3.11C.
Meanwhile, September as a whole recorded the highest monthly Niño3.4 region temperature anomaly – 2.84C – since sea surface temperature records began in the mid-1800s.
Hausfather wrote on CB Connect that this year’s El Niño had been “running well above any prior El Niño event since June, at times by a full degree [Celsius]”.

articles.title: China’s quarterly CO2 falls 3% in largest drop since Covid
articles.description: China’s carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions fell by 3.1% in the third quarter of 2026, as the Hormuz crisis continued to hit oil demand and coal use also dropped.
paragraphs: This was the largest quarterly reduction since the 2022 Covid lockdowns and means that China’s CO2 emissions have now fallen by an estimated 0.5% in the year to date.
The new analysis for Carbon Brief, based on official figures and commercial data, shows that coal use fell by 3% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, while oil was down 4%.
The main drivers were a fall in power-sector coal consumption, a continued sharp reduction in transport oil consumption and slowing growth in the coal-to-chemical industry.
The sharp decline in China’s CO2 emissions extends a “ flat or falling ” trend that began in March 2024 and has now lasted more than two years, as shown in the figure below.
The outlook for China’s CO2 emissions depends on the balance between rising energy demand, clean-energy growth and the government response to a GDP slowdown .
Key drivers of the fall in CO2 in the third quarter of 2026 included a 3.3% drop in coal-power generation, after demand growth slowed and the amount of “ wasted ” wind and solar fell.

Power generation from solar, wind and nuclear increased by 110 terawatt hours (TWh) year-on-year, more than twice as much as the growth in total electricity demand. This added clean-power generation equal to Germany’s total power output in the same time period.

The fall in coal-power output and CO2 emissions came despite the fact that China continues to build new coal-power capacity at near-record rates . This means that average running hours for coal plants are falling even faster than total generation, eroding their profits.

Meanwhile, transport oil consumption continued to fall sharply, down 9% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026. Electric vehicles (EVs) continued to gain market share, hitting a record 67% of passenger car sales and 50% of heavy trucks in September.

articles.title: Turkey must make COP31 a turning point for global climate action
articles.description: Turkey, which bridges developed and developing economies, is well placed to build consensus and partnerships at the Antalya summit - but it can set a better example at home too
paragraphs: Özgür Özel is the leader of Turkey's main opposition “New Party” and a member of parliament from Manisa.

For many people in Turkey, the climate crisis is already part of daily life. In 2021, forests in Manavgat, a district of Antalya, burned for more than a week. Last year, wildfires forced more than 50,000 people from their homes around the western coast city of Izmir. articles.title: Interactive: Tracking negotiating texts at the COP31 climate summit
articles.description: The centrepiece of every UN climate summit is for countries to negotiate the wording of a large number of legal agreements – and COP31 in the Turkish city of Antalya is no different.
paragraphs: These texts are hashed out behind closed doors in the “ blue zone ” at the COP, where diplomats from nearly 200 nations – not including the US – will be haggling over each individual verb .
Over the course of the two-week summit, negotiators will be trying to reach consensus on more than 100 separate agreements – but, first, they must agree which issues are on the agenda.
The complexity of this process can make it challenging to keep track of what countries are fighting about and how negotiations are progressing.
Carbon Brief’s real-time text tracker, below, offers a helping hand by decoding the agenda and keeping a searchable record of every document for each part of the negotiations.
The first column of the interactive tracker lists the topic of each agenda item, with further columns including dates, page counts and links to the original PDFs.
The table is searchable via the interactive text box and can be sorted using the arrow icons.
This year’s talks come with a twist: Turkey holds the presidency and is hosting COP31, but Australia is jointly running the show as “ president of negotiations ”.
The pair have already announced their intention to produce a “cover text” – an overarching political document summarising key negotiated outcomes, along with issues not on the official agenda.

This could include a recognition that warming is set to “ overshoot ” the 1.5C limit and the impacts this is already causing . It may also include potential solutions, such as the Turkish presidency’s “ electrification ” target, for 35% of global final energy to come from electricity by 2035.
articles.lede: The centrepiece of every UN climate summit is for countries to negotiate the wording of a large number of legal agreements – and COP31 in the Turkish city of Antalya is no different.

articles.title: COP31 Briefing: What to expect from the Antalya climate summit?
articles.description: Electrification, the fossil fuel transition, adaptation to rising impacts, climate science and trade are key themes as governments gather for COP31 in Türkiye
paragraphs: Here's an overview of issues to watch as governments, businesses and civil society head to the Turkish seaside resort of Antalya for two weeks of negotiations, leaders’ speeches, panel discussions and initiative launches.
This is the first COP to be staring an almost certain overshoot of the 1.5C warming limit in the face, even as countries squabble over when the next UN science reports should be delivered.

The geopolitical mood ahead of the annual talks, from November 9-20, has been sweetened somewhat by Lula’s surprise re-election in Brazil and American voters delivering a thumbs down to climate change-sceptic Donald Trump in the US midterms this week.

Here's an overview of issues to watch as governments, businesses and civil society head to the Turkish seaside resort of Antalya for two weeks of negotiations, leaders’ speeches, panel discussions and initiative launches.
This is the first COP to be staring an almost certain overshoot of the 1.5C warming limit in the face, even as countries squabble over when the next UN science reports should be delivered.

The geopolitical mood ahead of the annual talks, from November 9-20, has been sweetened somewhat by Lula’s surprise re-election in Brazil and American voters delivering a thumbs down to climate change-sceptic Donald Trump in the US midterms this week.

Still, neither of those things will make the talks much easier in practice, as fossil fuel-producing emerging economies are unlikely to want to make compromises on issues such as the energy transition and donor nations aren’t expected to turn up with much additional money for helping developing countries deal with worsening climate impacts.

With government budgets squeezed by ongoing conflicts and oil prices riding high after the Strait of Hormuz crisis, there will be a focus on the national benefits of boosting renewables, from a security and cost perspective. This advances the cause of the voluntary electrification goal proposed by Türkiye - which could be one of the biggest headlines from this COP.

In terms of the mechanics of how COP31 will work, all eyes are on the relationship between the co-hosts Türkiye and Australia. This unusual splitting of the presidency roles wasn’t born out of love, despite the friendly demeanour the country’s two environment ministers displayed at the pre-COP in Fiji.

The deal, for Türkiye to host the COP on its soil and run the non-negotiated Action Agenda side of things while Australia manages the formal negotiations, was reached last year after Ankara steadfastly refused to back down in the face of greater support for its rival. It’s all smiles for now, with Australia backing the Turkish-championed electrification goal and early signalling in Fiji that both COP31 teams will work on producing a COP cover decision, summarising key outcomes and setting the political direction for the year ahead.

articles.title: Climate Diplomacy Brief: COP31 preview
articles.description: Will US midterms & Lula’s win in Brazil deliver a COP31 bounce?
paragraphs: One vision “Wake up, wake up, put your hand on your heart before time is up.” Two minutes into one of the latest musical posts by the COP31 team it occurred to me that perhaps they think they’re hosting Eurovision, not a two-week climate summit involving 190+ countries and 50+ world leaders. Maybe that’s for the best. Another COP31 top tune’s lyrics include “ bring down the heat… let’s COP… take it to the top ”. Who says AI is bad for songwriting?

Context The UN’s annual review of national climate plans (aka NDCs) dropped on 27 Oct. 154 countries have lodged 2035 targets with the UN. Submitted plans cover 71% of global emissions (excluding land use). The good: the quality of plans is much better, legislation is tighter, tracking is clearer. The bad: “progress in lowering projected emissions [from the 1.5C targets] remains substantially off track” warns the UN.

Expectations Ignore for a moment the deluge of LinkedIn short-form videos building Antalya up as a huge moment. Two weeks in an exhibition hall won’t change global politics. “No single COP can fix this global crisis, but each takes meaningful steps forward”, UN climate chief Stiell said on 21 Sept. Despite the shadow of record heat, lethal glacier collapse and extreme weather, progress in Antalya will be incremental. This is the UN, not Usain Bolt.
Bookmark *Carbon Brief: Who wants what at COP31? *NRDC: International climate finance tracker *CAT: GHG analysis of all major emitters * ENB: Priceless daily update from inside the talks

1.5C “Countries cannot waffle on or walk away from 1.5”, reads a punchy pre-COP note from the 39-strong Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS). With the UNEP ‘ Limiting overshoot ’ report warning the 1.5C threshold is set to be breached, small islands are worried. And angry. Ditching 1.5C would be ‘egregious’ they say. They will hold ‘historical emitters and developed countries’ to account. ‘COP31 must be a reckoning’, they warn. Buckle up.

Presidency goals Ankara’s priorities are evident in its agenda for the 11-12 Nov Leaders Summit: electrification, green industrialisation, finance, zero waste and methane. And we know both Australia and Türkiye plan an overarching cover decision at the end to “recognise… bring profile… reaffirm” key issues. The emphasis is more on sending signals than on brokering major political shifts, which makes sense given the unstable state of the world.

Benchmarks So what could we reasonably expect, given fast rising greenhouse gas emissions need to be cut 18% by 2030, according to the latest UNEP Emissions Gap report? Below are 7 tests for COP31 that we’ll use to assess progress (and yes, I’m sure 4 won’t happen, but if you insist on hosting a climate summit there are some basic asks you should expect).

1. Is finance allocated by COP31 to Nepal for reconstruction/early warning? 2. Is there a clean electrification goal? Does it include $$$, grids & policies? 3. Are new fossil fuel phaseout plans published by governments? 4. Do hosts Türkiye & Australia commit to curbing coal use/exports? 5. Is there a plan to triple adaptation finance (as agreed in 2025)? 6. Have countries agreed (in negotiations) on how Global Stocktake 2 will work? 7. Will the IPCC deliver its next blockbuster report by GST2/2028?
articles.lede: Will US midterms & Lula’s win in Brazil deliver a COP31 bounce?

articles.title: Clean power shields China from oil shock more than any other country
articles.description: Rapid clean power growth and electrification have boosted China's energy resilience as well as its confidence in its energy policy pre-COP31, experts say
paragraphs: China’s rapidly-expanding clean energy generation and deepening electrification has made the country more resilient to energy shocks, bolstering its position ahead of the COP31 climate talks in Türkiye, where speeding up the world’s electrification is set to dominate.

“Yet, the import reduction did not produce the economic and social disruption in China one might normally expect from a shock of this scale,” the report found.
As temporary adjustment cushioned the oil-import shock, clean power and the electrification of the transport sector buffered the economic costs.

“China remains exposed to imported fuels, particularly where oil is used as a chemical feedstock, but reducing fossil-fuel demand already contributes to energy security,” said Qi Qin, the report’s author.

CREA’s analysis found the roll-out of electric vehicles (EVs) displaced 38 million tonnes of oil equivalent between March and August, equivalent to around 13% of China’s crude oil imports in the same period the previous year.

articles.title: Q&A: What is the Brazil-led ‘deforestation roadmap’?
articles.description: Carbon Brief explains where the deforestation roadmap came from, what it entails, why some did not sign on – and what’s next.
paragraphs: On 3 November, the Brazilian presidency of the COP30 climate talks released its long-awaited “roadmap” on ending deforestation.
Ahead of the Belém summit, Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva made a call for a “roadmap” to halt and reverse deforestation.
Although this voluntary roadmap was outside the COP’s official agenda, it snowballed into a rallying point at the “Amazon” COP.
Some 93 countries called for a reference to a new roadmap for ending deforestation to be part of COP30’s formal negotiated outcome.

However, at the end of the summit, the COP30 presidency announced that there was not the consensus needed for the deforestation roadmap to be part of the final text – but that Brazil would work to create a voluntary roadmap outside of the UN climate process.
This call was answered by 18 countries and four negotiating blocs that offered their inputs on the roadmap, along with scores of NGOs, research centres and other groups.
Now that the roadmap has been published, Carbon Brief explains where it came from, what it entails, why some did not sign on – and what’s next.
The “deforestation roadmap” was one of the signature announcements of the Brazilian presidency of the COP30 climate summit in Belém – albeit one that fell outside the official, negotiated outcomes.
Brazilian president Lula first proposed the deforestation and forest degradation roadmap, alongside one on the fossil fuel transition , at the leaders’ summit in Belém a few days before COP30 began.
By the end of COP30, nearly 100 countries had expressed their support for such a roadmap. This includes the EU, with its 27 member states, as well as the 56-member Coalition for Rainforest Nations .
articles.lede: Carbon Brief explains where the deforestation roadmap came from, what it entails, why some did not sign on – and what’s next.

articles.title: Q&A: What is in the global ‘roadmap’ for transitioning away from fossil fuels?
articles.description: Transitioning away from fossil fuels is “urgent, inevitable and, yet, possible”, says a first-of-its-kind global “roadmap” produced by Brazil.
paragraphs: The host of last year’s climate summit, COP30 , has set out a voluntary plan for how countries can move away from coal, oil and gas.
The roadmap says there is no “one-size-fits-all” approach to transitioning away from fossil fuels and asks countries to “diagnose” their own “readiness” to start the process.
After mapping out their specific circumstances, countries should then pursue “tailored levers” to take action, according to the roadmap.
These efforts should culminate by 2033, it says – 10 years on from when the COP28 climate summit in Dubai called on all countries to contribute to a global transition away from fossil fuels.
Below, Carbon Brief examines what the roadmap says and how it could influence debates about fossil fuels at the upcoming COP31 climate summit, which begins next week in Turkey.
Calls for a global “roadmap” away from fossil fuels dominated debates at COP30, which was held in the Amazonian city of Belém.
A group of 85 countries called for a reference to a new roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels to be part of COP30’s formal negotiated outcome.
This call came after the first “global stocktake” of action towards the world’s climate goals at COP28 in 2023 asked all countries to contribute to transitioning away from fossil fuels.

It was claimed that this group included 84 countries. However, Carbon Brief’s analysis of the “informal list” revealed inconsistencies and errors, meaning the total number of countries opposing the roadmap was likely smaller.
articles.lede: Transitioning away from fossil fuels is “urgent, inevitable and, yet, possible”, says a first-of-its-kind global “roadmap” produced by Brazil.

articles.title: CB Live: Carbon Brief’s team at COP17 on the nature talks’ key outcomes
articles.description: Following this year’s UN COP17 biodiversity conference, Carbon Brief’s journalists hosted a livestream to explain what happened at the summit.
paragraphs: Carbon Brief’s Orla Dwyer and Aruna Chandrasekhar have been on the ground in Yerevan, Armenia, over the past two weeks, covering the negotiations.
They were joined on the livestream by associate editors Dr Giuliana Viglione and Daisy Dunne , who were following the talks from Washington DC and London, respectively.
Carbon Brief has also published its 10,000-word explainer of COP17, which lays out the key outcomes in detail.
Orla and Aruna kicked off the livestream by explaining the biggest issues at the event, including biodiversity finance and the first “global review” of progress towards reversing nature loss.

The four journalists then took live questions from the audience in an “ask me anything” format, covering issues such as “ nature-harming subsidies ”, marine biodiversity and the status of the Cali fund , which is meant to raise private-sector finance.

articles.title: September 2026 Temperature Update
articles.description: August 2026 was the warmest August on record. El Niño is strengthening rapidly and expected to break all-time records. 2026 is likely to be a new record warmest year.
paragraphs: The following is a summary of global temperature conditions in Berkeley Earth’s analysis of September 2026.

According to Berkeley Earth’s high-resolution temperature dataset, September 2026 was the 2 nd warmest September since records began in 1850, with a monthly global average of 1.65 ± 0.11 °C (2.96 ± 0.19 °F) above the 1850–1900 (pre-industrial) average. It sits about 0.06 °C below September 2023. The anomaly in September 2026 is nominally the third largest of any month, behind only September 2023 and August 2026.

On a month-to-month basis, September was nominally slightly cooler than August 2026 though within the margin or error. It remains sharply warmer than other months in 2026. September 2026 continued the run of months above the 1.5 °C mark that began in July, as the warming influence of El Niño has grown.

Only one month of 2026 has set a record warm month (August 2026) with most months entering as the 2 nd to 5 th warmest. Depsite that, we have now pushed close to all-time record high temperature anomalies. Record and near-record warmth is expected to continue through the end of the year due to the short-term influence of a record-breaking El Niño.

Over the most recent 12 months (October 2025 to September 2026), the global average was 1.458 ± 0.074 °C (2.62 ± 0.13 °F) above the 1850–1900 average, making it the 2 nd warmest such 12-month period on record. It is behind the period ending in September 2024 and effectively tied with the period ending in September 2025, which it exceeds by only 0.003 °C. Because El Niño’s influence on the global mean lags its peak in the Pacific, this measure is expected to keep rising into 2027.

In September 2026, warmer-than-average temperatures covered most of the globe. The warmth was most pronounced across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, where El Niño appears as a broad warm band stretching east to the coast of South America, and across the high Arctic, including the Canadian Arctic Archipelago. Large positive anomalies also covered western and central Europe and the western Mediterranean, the western North Atlantic off North America, Australia, and much of northern and central Asia. Some of the largest anomalies anywhere were over West Antarctica. The most prominent cool anomaly was elsewhere on Antarctica, centered on the Weddell Sea sector and stretching along parts of the East Antarctic coast, with smaller cool areas over the Greenland ice sheet, along the west coast of the United States, and at the southern tip of South America.

Roughly 11.5% of Earth’s surface experienced its locally warmest September on record (about 9.3% of land and 12.7% of ocean surfaces), and 80.3% of the surface was warmer than average. The largest contiguous region of record warmth occurred in the Eastern tropical Pacific, where a record-breaking El Niño event is underway. Record warmth also covered parts of the tropical and western North Atlantic including the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean, Iberia and the western Mediterranean, northwest Africa, the Sahel and the Horn of Africa, the Arabian Peninsula and the Persian Gulf, much of the Indian Ocean, maritime Southeast Asia, and parts of northern Russia and Kazakhstan. Record and near-record warmth in tropical South America, Africa, and Southeast Asia are common features during large El Niño events.
articles.lede: August 2026 was the warmest August on record. El Niño is strengthening rapidly and expected to break all-time records.

articles.title: Introducing Berkeley Earth’s Data Pipeline 2.0
articles.description: A rebuilt, expanded and more resilient foundation for the Berkeley Earth temperature record. paragraphs: For fifteen years stakeholders from across the climate, resilience, and research ecosystems have come to Berkeley Earth for a clear, transparent, and trustworthy read on how our climate is changing. Much of that trust rests on work that has, until very recently, remained relatively invisible: the data pipeline that gathers, merges, and quality-checks millions of observations from more than 50,000 global weather stations every month.

Following a number of upstream data disruptions last year, Berkeley Earth made a commitment to invest in building a more resilient and robust data pipeline, one less dependent on any one single upstream source of observations, and one that could maintain crucial data continuity in the case that any single ingest product was disrupted or lost.

Today we’re excited to announce the launch of Berkeley Earth’s newly rebuilt pipeline 2.0 , not only reinforced but expanded to provide not only the most comprehensive but also the most resilient observational temperature record available. Below is an overview of what we improved, what hasn’t changed, and why this matters for the greater climate and resilience ecosystem.

The rebuilt pipeline is faster by design, which means earlier monthly updates going forward, and we expect to have near-real-time data flowing into Synthesis , our high-resolution climate platform, available within the next few months.

Along with this rebuild, Berkeley Earth’s full station archive is now open on Synthesis , made available for researchers, analysts, and anyone who wants to get their hands on the data behind the record. A few key stats about our world-leading station data archive:
